1.subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination and Percentage Composition
1.solution: In \(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}\), 2 Al (\(54\) g) go with 3 S (\(96\) g). For 4 g of sulfur: \(\dfrac{4 \times 54}{96} = 2.25\) g of aluminium.

2.solution: A completely filled 3d subshell is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves into 3d: Cu is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^1\).

4.subtopic: Group 16 Chalcogens, Oxygen, Sulphur and Ozone
4.solution: Down group 16 the E-H bond becomes longer and weaker, so the hydride gives up \(\mathrm{H^+}\) more easily: \(\mathrm{H_2S < H_2Se < H_2Te}\).

5.subtopic: Molecular Orbital Theory and Bond Order
5.solution: In \(\mathrm{O_2}\) the two \(\pi^*2p\) orbitals hold one electron each (Hund's rule), so it has two unpaired electrons and is paramagnetic. \(\mathrm{Li_2}\), \(\mathrm{N_2}\) and \(\mathrm{F_2}\) have all electrons paired.

6.subtopic: Real Gases, Dalton's Law and KTG
6.solution: An ideal gas is a model: it obeys the gas laws exactly, its collisions are perfectly elastic and its molecules do not attract each other. No real gas behaves like this at all conditions, so an ideal gas does not actually exist.

8.subtopic: First Law of Thermodynamics, Internal Energy and Work
8.solution: \(q = -4\) kJ (released) and \(W = +12\) kJ (done on the system), so \(\Delta U = q + W = 8\) kJ. The heat exchanged at constant pressure is the enthalpy change: \(\Delta H = -4\) kJ.

9.subtopic: Enthalpy and Relation Between ΔH and ΔU
9.solution: One mole of gas is used and one formed, so \(\Delta n_g = 0\) and \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT = \Delta U\).

11.solution: The common ion fixes \([\mathrm{Cl^-}] \approx 0.1\) M, so \(S = \dfrac{K_{sp}}{[\mathrm{Cl^-}]} = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{-10}}{0.1} = 1.8 \times 10^{-9}\) M.

12.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium, Ka, Kb and Degree of Dissociation
12.solution: Aqueous ammonia ionises only partly, \(\mathrm{NH_3 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons NH_4^+ + OH^-}\), so it is a weak electrolyte. NaOH, KOH and HI dissociate completely.

14.subtopic: Subatomic Particles, Isotopes, Isobars and Isoelectronic Species
14.solution: Hydrogen makes up about three quarters of the ordinary matter in the universe.

15.subtopic: Group 2 Alkaline Earth Metals, Properties and Reactivity
15.solution: Chlorine passed over dry slaked lime gives bleaching powder: \(\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2 + Cl_2 \rightarrow CaOCl_2 + H_2O}\).

16.solution: An aromatic alcohol has its OH group on a side chain carbon (\(sp^3\)) attached to the ring, as in II (benzyl alcohol) and III (3-ethylbenzyl alcohol). In I and IV the OH is directly on the ring, so they are phenols.

17.subtopic: Carboxylic Acids, Properties, Reactions and Derivatives
17.solution: Oxidative rancidity of fats and oils is the attack of oxygen on the unsaturated chains by a free radical chain mechanism (initiation, propagation, termination), giving peroxides and then foul-smelling aldehydes and acids.

18.subtopic: Electronic Effects, Hybridization, Intermediates and General Reactions
18.solution: \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH^+}\) has two methyl groups next to the positive carbon, with \(3 + 3 = 6\) \(\alpha\)-hydrogens. Each gives one hyperconjugation structure: 6.

19.subtopic: Nomenclature, Hybridization and Stability of Alkenes
19.solution: Alkyl groups stabilise a double bond (by hyperconjugation), so the more substituted the alkene, the more stable. The tetrasubstituted \(\mathrm{R_2C{=}CR_2}\) is the most stable.

20.subtopic: Preparation of Alkanes, Wurtz, Grignard and Decarboxylation
20.solution: The couplings are ethyl-ethyl (n-butane), ethyl-propyl (n-pentane) and propyl-propyl (n-hexane). Propane cannot form.

21.solution: Close packing gives two tetrahedral voids per particle: \(2 \times 0.8 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 9.635 \times 10^{23}\).

22.solution: \(\rho a^3\) is the mass of one unit cell, so 90 g holds \(\dfrac{90}{1.8 \times 10^{-22}} = 5 \times 10^{23}\) cells. With 2 atoms per bcc cell, that is \(1.0 \times 10^{24}\) atoms.

23.solution: An fcc cell has 4 spheres and 8 tetrahedral voids, so there are 2 tetrahedral holes per sphere.

24.solution: By Raoult's law \(P = x_1P^0\). The vapour pressure is \(80\%\) of \(P^0\), so \(x_1 = 0.8\).

25.solution: Molality \(= \dfrac{18/180}{0.100} = 1\) mol/kg, so \(\Delta T_b = 0.5 \times 1 = 0.5\) K. The boiling point is \(100.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

26.solution: Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles: osmotic pressure, lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point and depression of freezing point. Vapour pressure, boiling point and freezing point themselves are not colligative; osmotic pressure is.

27.subtopic: Galvanic Cells, EMF, Nernst Equation and Thermodynamics
27.solution: Standard electrode potentials are quoted as reduction potentials, so \(+0.34\) V refers to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}\).

28.solution: Depositing one mole of Fe needs 2 F from \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) and 3 F from \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\). The same charge Q gives \(\dfrac{Q}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{Q}{3}\) moles, a ratio of \(3 : 2\).

29.subtopic: Batteries, Primary, Secondary and Fuel Cells
29.solution: On discharge \(\mathrm{Pb + PbO_2 + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2PbSO_4 + 2H_2O}\): sulphuric acid is consumed and \(\mathrm{PbSO_4}\) is formed (the acid density falls).

30.subtopic: Temperature Dependence, Arrhenius and Collision Theory

31.subtopic: Rate Law, Order, Molecularity and Rate Expression
31.solution: The unit \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) shows a first order reaction, rate \(= k[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]\). So \([\mathrm{N_2O_5}] = \dfrac{2.4 \times 10^{-5}}{3.0 \times 10^{-5}} = 0.8\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}\).

32.subtopic: First-Order Kinetics, Rate Constant and Half-Life
32.solution: The rate of radioactive decay is proportional to the number of nuclei present, \(-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N\): first order.

33.solution: Nanomaterials are used in scratch-proof coatings, electronic devices and self-cleaning surfaces. Conventional water treatment (coagulation, filtration, chlorination) does not use them.

34.subtopic: Colloids, Classification, Coagulation and Hardy-Schulze Rule
34.solution: The colour of a colloid depends on how its particles scatter light, which depends on their size: the same scattering of light by colloidal particles that causes the Tyndall effect.

35.subtopic: Colour, Magnetic Properties and Spin-Only Formula
35.solution: A partly filled d subshell lets an electron absorb visible light and jump between d orbitals split by the ligands. The colour seen is the complement of the light absorbed in these d-d transitions.

36.subtopic: Bonding Theories, EAN, Crystal Field, Hybridization and Magnetism
36.solution: \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\). With \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) the six electrons pair in the \(t_{2g}\) set (low spin), leaving 0 unpaired electrons, and the six ligands give an octahedral (\(d^2sp^3\)) complex.

37.subtopic: Oxidation State, Coordination Number and IUPAC Nomenclature
37.solution: The complex ion is \(2+\) (balanced by \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\)). With neutral \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{Br^-}\): \(x - 1 = +2\), so \(x = +3\).

38.solution: \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) needs backside attack, which bulky groups block. The rate falls methyl \(> 1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ\), so methyl bromide reacts fastest.

39.solution: All four give the same tert-butyl carbocation, so the rate is set by how easily the halide leaves. The C-I bond is the weakest and iodide the best leaving group.

40.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Alcohols and Acidity
40.solution: Alcohols are far weaker acids than water and do not ionise appreciably in it, so their aqueous solutions are neutral to litmus.

41.solution: Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate) oxidises an aldehyde and is itself reduced to metallic silver, which coats the tube as a silver mirror on warming. (A) is Schiff's test and (C) Fehling's test.

42.solution:
\(\mathrm{H_2/Ni}\) reduces both the C=C and the CHO group: P is pentan-1-ol, \(\mathrm{CH_3(CH_2)_3CH_2OH}\).

\(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) reduces the carbonyl group but leaves an isolated C=C untouched: Q is \(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCH_2CH_2OH}\).

43.subtopic: Nomenclature and Classification of Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
43.solution: HCOOH (methanoic acid) is commonly called formic acid; it was first obtained from ants (Latin formica).

44.subtopic: Diazonium Salts and Aromatic Amine Reactions
44.solution: In the Sandmeyer reaction a diazonium salt is converted to an aryl halide (or cyanide) with a copper(I) salt. The Mendius, Hofmann and carbylamine reactions start from nitriles, amides and amines.

45.solution: Isopropylamine, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHNH_2}\), has N attached to one carbon group, so it is a primary amine; (D) is wrong. Amine class depends on the groups on nitrogen, which is also why tert-butylamine is primary.

46.subtopic: Nucleic Acids, DNA, RNA, Nucleotides and Bases
46.solution: The backbone is alternating sugar and phosphate units joined by phosphodiester links (phosphate-sugar-phosphate); the bases hang from the sugars.

47.solution: The haem groups of haemoglobin hold \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), which binds oxygen reversibly and carries it.

48.solution: Vulcanization heats rubber with sulphur, forming sulphur cross-links between the polymer chains.

49.solution: Polymers are classified by source (natural, synthetic), structure (linear, branched, cross-linked), method of preparation (addition, condensation), intermolecular forces and kind of monomers (homo- or co-polymer). The number of monomer units is not a basis of classification.

50.subtopic: Colloids, Classification, Coagulation and Hardy-Schulze Rule
50.solution: Cationic detergents, quaternary ammonium salts such as cetyltrimethylammonium bromide, have germicidal properties and are used as disinfectants.

52.subtopic: Modulus and Argument — Polar Form, De Moivre and Square Roots
52.solution: Taking the square of the modulus of both sides: \(|1 + i|^2|1 + 2i|^2\cdots|1 + ni|^2 = (2)(5)(10)\cdots(1 + n^2) = x^2 + y^2\).

53.subtopic: Counting Numbers and Geometric Figures — Digits, Divisibility, Points and Polygons
53.solution:
Two-digit numbers: first digit 6 ways (not 0), second 6 ways: 36. Three-digit numbers: \(6 \times 6 \times 5 = 180\). Total 216.

"Strictly between 10 and 1000" excludes 10 itself, which is one of the two-digit numbers counted. So the answer is \(215\).

54.solution:
\(\dfrac{\sin 3A}{\sin A} = 3 - 4\sin^2 A\) and \(\dfrac{\cos 3A}{\cos A} = 4\cos^2 A - 3\).

Their difference is \(6 - 4 = 2\) and their sum \(4\cos^2 A - 4\sin^2 A = 4\cos 2A\). The expression, a difference of squares, is \(2 \times 4\cos 2A = 8\cos 2A\).

55.solution:
\(\sin x + \sin 3x = 2\sin 2x\cos x\), so the equation is \(\sin 2x(2\cos x - 1) = 0\).

\(\sin 2x = 0\) gives \(x = 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\); \(\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}\) gives \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\). Three values.

56.subtopic: Forms of a Line, Intersections and Concurrency
56.solution: Intercepts a and \(-a\) (\(a \neq 0\)): \(\dfrac{x}{a} - \dfrac{y}{a} = 1\), that is \(x - y = a\). Through \((3, 4)\): \(a = -1\). Only one such line, \(x - y + 1 = 0\).

57.subtopic: Slopes of a Homogeneous Pair — Sum, Product and Ratio Conditions

58.subtopic: Tangents — At a Point, With a Given Slope, From an External Point and Their Loci
58.solution: A parallel line is \(2x + y = c\). Its distance from the centre equals the radius: \(\dfrac{|c|}{\sqrt{5}} = \sqrt{10}\), so \(c = \pm 5\sqrt{2}\).

60.solution:
For small x: \((5^x - 1)^4 \approx x^4(\log 5)^4\), \(\mathrm{cosec}(x\log 5) \approx \dfrac{1}{x\log 5}\), \(\tan(x\log 5) \approx x\log 5\) and \(\log(1 + x^2\log 25) \approx 2x^2\log 5\).

The limit is \(\dfrac{x^4(\log 5)^4}{x\log 5 \cdot x\log 5 \cdot 2x^2\log 5} = \dfrac{\log 5}{2} = \log\sqrt{5}\).

61.solution:
The three parallel branches give \((s_1 \wedge s_2) \vee (s_1 \wedge \sim s_2) \vee (\sim s_1 \wedge s_2)\).

The first two combine to \(s_1 \wedge (s_2 \vee \sim s_2) = s_1\), and \(s_1 \vee (\sim s_1 \wedge s_2) = s_1 \vee s_2\). So \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) in parallel, circuit B.

62.subtopic: Solution of Triangle — Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
62.solution:
\(b\cos^2\dfrac{C}{2} + c\cos^2\dfrac{B}{2} = \dfrac{b + c}{2} + \dfrac{b\cos C + c\cos B}{2} = \dfrac{b + c + a}{2}\) (projection rule).

\(\dfrac{a + b + c}{2} = \dfrac{3a}{2}\) gives \(b + c = 2a\): b, a, c are in A.P.

63.subtopic: Solution of Triangle — Half-Angle Formulas, Napier's Analogy and Area
63.solution: Napier's analogy: \(\tan\dfrac{A - B}{2} = \dfrac{a - b}{a + b}\cot\dfrac{C}{2} = \dfrac{2}{2\sqrt{3}} \times \sqrt{3} = 1\), so \(A - B = 90^\circ\). With \(A + B = 120^\circ\): \(A = 105^\circ\), \(B = 15^\circ\).

64.subtopic: Inverse of a Matrix — Adjoint Formula, Products and Verification
64.solution: The determinant is \(12 + 2 = 14\), so the inverse is \(\dfrac{1}{14}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{2}{7} & \frac{1}{7} \\ -\frac{1}{14} & \frac{3}{14} \end{bmatrix}\).

65.subtopic: Determinants, Cofactors and the Adjoint Identities

66.solution: Put \(x = \sin\theta\): the bracket is \(\dfrac{\sin\theta - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta + \cos\theta} = \tan\left(\theta - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\), so \(y = \sin^{-1}x - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}\).

67.subtopic: Inverse Trigonometric Functions — Principal Values and Evaluation

68.subtopic: Inverse Trigonometric Identities — Sums, Substitution and Telescoping
68.solution:
\(\sin^{-1}\dfrac{12}{13} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{12}{5}\) and \(\cos^{-1}\dfrac{4}{5} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{3}{4}\). Their sum has tangent \(\dfrac{12/5 + 3/4}{1 - 9/5} = -\dfrac{63}{16}\) and, since \(\dfrac{12}{5}\cdot\dfrac{3}{4} > 1\), lies in \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)\): it is \(\pi - \tan^{-1}\dfrac{63}{16}\).

Adding \(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{63}{16}\) gives \(\pi\).

69.subtopic: Composite Functions — f∘g, Iteration and Functional Identities
69.solution: \(f(f(x)) = \dfrac{4f + 3}{6f - 4}\), with \(4f + 3 = \dfrac{34x}{6x - 4}\) and \(6f - 4 = \dfrac{34}{6x - 4}\), so \(g(x) = x\). Any number of applications of g leaves 3 unchanged.

70.subtopic: Continuity of Piecewise Functions — Junction Conditions and Parameter Systems
70.solution:
f must be continuous at \(-1\): \(a + b = b - a + 4\), so \(a = 2\).

The derivatives must match: \(2a(-1) = 2b(-1) + a\), that is \(-4 = -2b + 2\), so \(b = 3\).

72.solution:
Put \(y^{1/m} = e^t\): \(x = \cosh t\), so \(y = e^{mt}\) with \(t = \cosh^{-1}x\).

\(y_1 = my\dfrac{dt}{dx} = \dfrac{my}{\sqrt{x^2 - 1}}\), hence \((x^2 - 1)y_1^2 = m^2y^2\).

73.subtopic: Rate of Change and Related Rates
73.solution: With \(C(x, x)\): \(s = \dfrac{1}{2}[a(b - x) + 0 + x(0 - b)] = \dfrac{1}{2}[ab - (a + b)x]\) (taking the orientation that is positive near the origin). So \(\dfrac{ds}{dx} = -\dfrac{a + b}{2}\).

74.solution: \(f'(x) = \dfrac{\cos x - \sin x}{1 + (\sin x + \cos x)^2}\), positive where \(\cos x > \sin x\), that is on \(\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\). Of the options, \(\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\) lies inside this.

75.solution: \(f'(x) = \dfrac{1 - \log x}{x^2}\): f rises on \((2, e)\) and falls for \(x > e\), tending to 0 as \(x \to \infty\) without reaching it. Near 2 the values approach \(\dfrac{\log 2}{2}\), also not attained. So f has a maximum \(\dfrac{1}{e}\) but no minimum on \((2, \infty)\).

76.solution: Put \(t = x + \log x\), \(dt = \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx = \dfrac{x + 1}{x}\,dx\). The integral is \(\displaystyle\int t^2\,dt = \dfrac{(x + \log x)^3}{3} + c\).

77.solution:
\(\cot^4 x = \cot^2 x\,\mathrm{cosec}^2 x - \cot^2 x = \cot^2 x\,\mathrm{cosec}^2 x - \mathrm{cosec}^2 x + 1\).

Integrating: \(-\dfrac{\cot^3 x}{3} + \cot x + x + c\).

78.subtopic: Trigonometric Integrals - Rational and Substitution Forms
78.solution: Put \(t = \sin x\): \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1 - t^2}{t(t + 1)}\,dt = \int\dfrac{1 - t}{t}\,dt = \log t - t + c = \log(\sin x) - \sin x + c\).

79.subtopic: King's Property — f(a + b − x) and the f/(f + g) Family
79.solution: Replacing x by \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\) keeps the limits and the denominator but changes the numerator to \(\cos x - \sin x\). So \(I = -I\) and \(I = 0\).

80.subtopic: Evaluating Definite Integrals — Standard Forms, Algebraic Substitution and By Parts
80.solution:
Put \(e^x - 1 = t^2\), \(e^x\,dx = 2t\,dt\); the limits become \(0\) to \(2\).

\(\displaystyle\int_0^2\dfrac{2t^2}{t^2 + 4}\,dt = 2\int_0^2\left(1 - \dfrac{4}{t^2 + 4}\right)dt = 2\left[t - 2\tan^{-1}\dfrac{t}{2}\right]_0^2 = 2\left(2 - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 4 - \pi\).

81.solution:
Rewrite with t as the variable: \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -\dfrac{x - e^{\tan^{-1}t}}{1 + t^2}\), that is \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} + \dfrac{x}{1 + t^2} = \dfrac{e^{\tan^{-1}t}}{1 + t^2}\).

The integrating factor is \(e^{\int\frac{dt}{1 + t^2}} = e^{\tan^{-1}t}\).

82.subtopic: Order, Degree, Formation of ODE, and Verification of Solutions
82.solution:
Differentiating: \(2(y - a)y' = 4\), so \(y - a = \dfrac{2}{y'}\). Differentiating again: \(y' = -\dfrac{2y''}{(y')^2}\), that is \(2y'' + (y')^3 = 0\).

The highest derivative \(y''\) appears to the first power: degree 1.

83.solution:
Treat x as a function of y: \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{x + 2y^3}{y}\), that is \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} - \dfrac{x}{y} = 2y^2\). The integrating factor is \(\dfrac{1}{y}\):

\(\dfrac{d}{dy}\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) = 2y\), so \(\dfrac{x}{y} = y^2 + c\) and \(x = (c + y^2)y\).

84.solution:
\(\dfrac{dA}{dt} = -k\sqrt{A}\) gives \(2\sqrt{A} = -kt + c\): \(\sqrt{A}\) falls uniformly.

\(\sqrt{A}\) goes from 100 to 75 in 2 years, 12.5 per year, so it reaches 0 after \(\dfrac{100}{12.5} = 8\) years.

85.solution: A rotation keeps the magnitude: \(9 + 16 + 25 = (a + 1)^2 + 9 + 25\), so \((a + 1)^2 = 16\) and \(a = 3\) or \(-5\).

86.subtopic: Vector Geometry — Section Formula, Triangle, and Parallelogram
86.solution:
\(\overline{AB} = \overline{DC} = (6, 1)\) and \(\overline{AD} = \overline{BC} = (-1, 3)\), so ABCD is a parallelogram.

\(\overline{AB}\cdot\overline{AD} = -6 + 3 = -3 \neq 0\), so it is not a rectangle, and \(|AB| = \sqrt{37} \neq |AD| = \sqrt{10}\), so it is not a rhombus.

88.subtopic: Angles — Line, Plane, and Direction Conditions
88.solution:
The plane's normal is \((2, 3, -1) \times (1, -1, 2) = (5, -5, -5)\), that is \((1, -1, -1)\).

The angle \(\theta\) between a vector and a plane has \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{|(2, 1, -3)\cdot(1, -1, -1)|}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{42}}\).

89.subtopic: Vector Geometry — Section Formula, Triangle, and Parallelogram
89.solution:
\(|\bar{a}|^2 = 8\), \(|\bar{b}|^2 = 9\) and \(\bar{a}\cdot\bar{b} = 2\sqrt{2} \times 3 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 6\). The diagonals are \(6\bar{a} - \bar{b}\) and \(4\bar{a} + 5\bar{b}\).

\(|6\bar{a} - \bar{b}|^2 = 288 - 72 + 9 = 225\) and \(|4\bar{a} + 5\bar{b}|^2 = 128 + 240 + 225 = 593\). The lengths are \(15\) and \(\sqrt{593}\).

91.subtopic: Angles — Line, Plane, and Direction Conditions
91.solution:
A plane through \((1, 0, 0)\) and \((0, 1, 0)\) is \(ax + ay + cz = a\), with normal \((a, a, c)\).

\(\cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{|2a + 3a|}{\sqrt{2a^2 + c^2}\sqrt{13}}\), so \(50a^2 = 13(2a^2 + c^2)\) and \(c^2 = \dfrac{24}{13}a^2\).

Taking \(a = \sqrt{13}\): \(c = \sqrt{24} = 2\sqrt{6}\). The direction ratios are \(\sqrt{13}, \sqrt{13}, 2\sqrt{6}\).

92.solution:
Directions \((-1, 1, -2)\) and \((1, 1, -2)\) are not parallel, and their dot product is \(-1 + 1 + 4 = 4 \neq 0\).

The points \((1, -2, 3)\) and \((1, -2, -1)\) differ by \((0, 0, -4)\), and the cross product of the directions is \((0, -4, -2)\). Since \((0, 0, -4)\cdot(0, -4, -2) = 8 \neq 0\), the lines do not meet: they are skew.

93.solution: Distance from the origin: \(\sqrt{14}\). Distance from the plane: \(\dfrac{|2 - 6 + 3 + k|}{\sqrt{14}} = \dfrac{|k - 1|}{\sqrt{14}}\). Their product \(|k - 1| = 7\) gives \(k = 8\) or \(-6\); only 8 is an option.

94.subtopic: Line — Equation, Direction Cosines, and Vector Form
94.solution: Along the line x stays 2 and \(2y = 3z - 7\), so the direction is \((0, 3, 2)\). With \(y = 0\), \(z = \dfrac{7}{3}\): the point \(\left(2, 0, \dfrac{7}{3}\right)\).

95.subtopic: Feasible Region — Half-Plane Tests, Bounded, Unbounded and Empty
95.solution: The region is bounded by \(x + y = 5\), \(y = 2\), \(x = 4\) and \(y = 2x + 4\). Its corners are \((3, 2)\), \((4, 2)\), \((4, 12)\) and \(\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{14}{3}\right)\): a bounded convex region with 4 corner points.

96.subtopic: Conditional Probability, Independence and Bayes' Theorem
96.solution: \(A = \{3, 5\}\), so \(P(A) = \dfrac{1}{3}\): p is true. \(B = \{1, 3, 5\}\), \(P(B) = \dfrac{1}{2}\), and \(A \cap B = A\) has probability \(\dfrac{1}{3} \neq \dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\): q is false.

97.subtopic: Classical Probability, Addition Theorem and Odds

98.subtopic: Discrete Random Variables, PMF and CDF

99.subtopic: Discrete Random Variables, PMF and CDF
99.solution: \(10k = 1\), so the probabilities are \(\dfrac{1}{10}, \dfrac{2}{10}, \dfrac{3}{10}, \dfrac{4}{10}\). The c.d.f. adds them up: \(\dfrac{1}{10}, \dfrac{3}{10}, \dfrac{6}{10}, 1\).

102.solution: \(\vec{P} - \vec{Q} = 2(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = 2\vec{P}\), which is parallel to \(\vec{P}\): the angle is \(0^\circ\).

103.subtopic: Kinematics — Equations of Motion, Free Fall, and Graphs
103.solution: The ball takes \(\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}\) to fall and the same to rise back to h, so the period is \(2\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}\) and the frequency \(\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{2h}}\).

104.solution: The boy from A runs straight to the meeting point, which is \(V_1t\) from B along the perpendicular. Pythagoras: \((Vt)^2 = a^2 + (V_1t)^2\), so \(t = \left[\dfrac{a^2}{V^2 - V_1^2}\right]^{1/2}\).

105.solution: Starting from rest, \(\omega = \alpha t\). Equal magnitudes: \(r\alpha = r\omega^2 = r\alpha^2t^2\), so \(t^2 = \dfrac{1}{\alpha} = \dfrac{1}{4}\) and \(t = 0.5\) s.

106.subtopic: Dynamics of Circular Motion — Banking, Conical Pendulum, Vertical Circle
106.solution:
The normal reaction is perpendicular to the cone's surface. With the circle at height h above the vertex and radius r, its vertical component balances mg and its horizontal component gives \(\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\), which leads to \(\dfrac{v^2}{r} = g\dfrac{h}{r}\), so \(h = \dfrac{v^2}{g}\).

\(h = \dfrac{0.25}{10} = 0.025\) m \(= 2.5\) cm.

107.solution: At maximum compression all the kinetic energy is in the spring: \(\dfrac{1}{2}Kx^2\). The block regains it all when the spring is back at its natural length, where its momentum is greatest: \(\dfrac{p^2}{2m} = \dfrac{1}{2}Kx^2\), so \(p = \sqrt{Km}\,x\).
